synonyms._comment: Search synonyms. A query containing a key is also searched with its value(s). Keys are lower case.

0.title: Why Bitcoin Matters Historically
0.summary: Bitcoin was the first working system to let an open network agree on a shared ledger of digital money without a central record keeper, and later projects built on that idea.
0.aliases: history of Bitcoin | Bitcoin significance | digital cash history | double-spending problem

1.title: Common Bitcoin Misconceptions
1.summary: Many popular statements about Bitcoin, from both enthusiasts and critics, are inaccurate. This page compares common claims with how the system actually works.
1.aliases: Bitcoin myths | Bitcoin facts | is Bitcoin anonymous | Bitcoin myths and facts

2.title: Fees & Block Space
2.summary: Bitcoin blocks have limited room, so transactions compete for it by offering fees. The fee depends on a transaction's data size, not on the amount being sent.
2.aliases: Bitcoin fees | transaction fee | fee rate | sat/vB | block size | block weight | miner fee

3.title: Genesis Block & Early History
3.summary: The genesis block is the first block of the Bitcoin blockchain, dated 3 January 2009. This page follows the network from that block through its first few years.
3.aliases: genesis block | block 0 | Bitcoin history | Bitcoin pizza | first Bitcoin transaction

4.title: Keys & Addresses
4.summary: In Bitcoin, a private key is the secret that authorises spending, a public key is derived from it, and an address is a shareable form used to receive payments.
4.aliases: Bitcoin address | private key | public key | digital signature | bc1 address | Bitcoin keys

5.title: The Lightning Network
5.summary: The Lightning Network is a second layer built on Bitcoin in which two parties lock funds in a shared channel and exchange many payments without recording each one on the blockchain.
5.aliases: Lightning | LN | payment channels | Bitcoin layer 2 | HTLC

6.title: Mempool & Confirmations
6.summary: The mempool is where valid Bitcoin transactions wait before a miner includes them in a block. Each block added after that counts as one confirmation.
6.aliases: mempool | memory pool | confirmations | unconfirmed transaction | six confirmations | pending transaction

7.title: Nodes & Decentralization
7.summary: A Bitcoin node is a computer that independently checks blocks and transactions against the rules. Decentralization describes how widely that checking is spread.
7.aliases: full node | Bitcoin node | light client | SPV | soft fork | hard fork | decentralisation

8.title: Proof of Work & Mining
8.summary: Mining is the process by which Bitcoin blocks are created. Miners compete to find a hash below a target, and that costly search is called proof of work.
8.aliases: Bitcoin mining | PoW | miners | hash rate | difficulty adjustment

9.title: Satoshi Nakamoto
9.summary: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the unidentified person or group who designed Bitcoin, wrote its white paper and released its first software.
9.aliases: Satoshi | Bitcoin creator | who created Bitcoin | Nakamoto

10.title: The 21 Million Limit
10.summary: Bitcoin's rules allow just under 21 million bitcoin to be created. The limit is the result of a block subsidy that halves every 210,000 blocks until it reaches zero.
10.aliases: 21 million bitcoin | Bitcoin supply cap | maximum supply | hard cap | satoshi unit

11.title: The Bitcoin White Paper
11.summary: The Bitcoin white paper is the nine-page document from 2008 in which Satoshi Nakamoto described how digital cash could work without a trusted third party.
11.aliases: Bitcoin whitepaper | Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System | Satoshi white paper

12.title: The Halving
12.summary: The halving is the scheduled event, every 210,000 blocks, at which the number of new bitcoin created with each block is cut in half.
12.aliases: Bitcoin halving | halvening | block reward halving | subsidy halving

13.title: The UTXO Model
13.summary: Bitcoin does not store account balances. It tracks unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs): discrete chunks of bitcoin that each transaction consumes and replaces.
13.aliases: UTXO | unspent transaction output | inputs and outputs | change output | UTXO set

14.title: What Is Bitcoin?
14.summary: Bitcoin is a digital currency and payment network that runs without a central operator, using a public ledger that thousands of independent computers verify.

15.title: Blocks & Hashes
15.summary: A block is a batch of transactions plus the hash of the previous block. A cryptographic hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of data, in which any change to the input changes the output.
15.aliases: block | hash | hash function | cryptographic hash | SHA-256 | block header | Merkle root | block height

16.title: Bridges
16.summary: A blockchain bridge moves value between two chains, usually by locking an asset on one and issuing a matching token on the other. Bridges have been frequent targets of large exploits.
16.aliases: bridge | blockchain bridge | cross-chain bridge | bridging | wrapped token | wrapped asset | lock and mint | cross-chain

17.title: Consensus
17.summary: Consensus is the process by which the independent computers of a blockchain network agree on a single history of transactions without relying on a central authority.
17.aliases: consensus mechanism | consensus algorithm | consensus protocol | fork choice | 51% attack | double spend | Byzantine fault tolerance | reorg

18.title: Finality & Throughput
18.summary: Finality is the point after which a transaction is practically irreversible. Throughput is how many transactions a chain processes per second. Both trade off against decentralisation and security.
18.aliases: finality | throughput | TPS | transactions per second | probabilistic finality | deterministic finality | confirmations | reorg | scalability trilemma | block time

19.title: Layer 1 & Layer 2
19.summary: A Layer 1 is a base blockchain that secures and settles transactions itself. A Layer 2 processes transactions off that base chain and settles the results to it, to increase capacity.
19.aliases: layer 1 | layer 2 | L1 | L2 | rollup | rollups | optimistic rollup | zk rollup | ZK-rollup | sequencer | sidechain | scaling

20.title: Nodes, Validators & Miners
20.summary: Nodes store and verify a blockchain's ledger. Miners, under proof of work, and validators, under proof of stake, are the participants that propose new blocks for the nodes to check.
20.aliases: node | full node | light client | miner | validator | block producer | mining pool | staking pool

21.title: Proof of Stake
21.summary: Proof of stake secures a blockchain with locked capital: validators deposit the network's coin as a stake, are chosen to propose and vote on blocks, and can lose that stake for misbehaving.
21.aliases: PoS | proof-of-stake | staking | validator | slashing | attestation | delegated proof of stake | liquid staking

22.title: Proof of Work
22.summary: Proof of work secures a blockchain by making block production cost computation and energy: miners compete to find a block hash below a target, and rewriting history means redoing that work.
22.aliases: PoW | proof-of-work | mining | hash rate | hashrate | mining difficulty | difficulty adjustment | nonce

23.title: Public & Private Blockchains
23.summary: A public blockchain lets anyone read, transact and help validate. A private or permissioned blockchain restricts those roles to approved participants chosen by an operator or consortium.
23.aliases: public blockchain | private blockchain | permissioned blockchain | permissionless blockchain | consortium blockchain | enterprise blockchain | permissioned ledger

24.title: Smart Contracts
24.summary: A smart contract is a program stored on a blockchain that runs exactly as written when a transaction calls it. Its code and balances are public, and bugs in it can be exploited.
24.aliases: smart contract | contract | on-chain program | dapp | decentralized application | Solidity | contract address

25.title: Transactions
25.summary: A blockchain transaction is a signed instruction, such as a transfer of value, that is broadcast to the network, checked by nodes and recorded in the ledger once it is in a block, and increasingly hard to reverse.
25.aliases: transaction | tx | txn | transaction hash | tx hash | txid | nonce | pending transaction | confirmations

26.title: What Is a Blockchain?
26.summary: A blockchain is a shared ledger in which records are grouped into blocks, each block is linked to the one before it by a cryptographic hash, and many independent computers hold a copy.
26.aliases: blockchain | block chain | distributed ledger | DLT | shared ledger

27.title: What Is Cryptocurrency?
27.summary: A cryptocurrency is a digital asset whose ownership records are kept on a blockchain, a shared ledger run by a network of computers instead of a single bank or company.
27.aliases: crypto | cryptocurrencies | digital currency | crypto asset | digital asset

28.title: Coin vs Token
28.summary: A coin is the native asset of its own blockchain. A token is an asset issued by a smart contract on a blockchain that already exists.
28.aliases: coins vs tokens | token vs coin | difference between coin and token | crypto coin or token

29.title: Layer 1 vs Layer 2
29.summary: A Layer 1 is a base blockchain with its own consensus. A Layer 2 processes transactions off that base chain and settles the results back to it, aiming for lower fees and higher capacity.
29.aliases: l1 vs l2 | layer 2 vs layer 1 | layer one vs layer two | l2 vs l1 | base layer vs rollup

30.title: Proof of Work vs Proof of Stake
30.summary: Proof of Work secures a blockchain with computation and energy. Proof of Stake secures it with locked-up coins. Both make it costly to rewrite the ledger.
30.aliases: pow vs pos | proof of stake vs proof of work | mining vs staking | pos vs pow

31.title: Assets & Asset Classes
31.summary: An asset is something of economic value that can be owned and traded. Asset classes are groups of assets that share the same basic features and behave in broadly similar ways.
31.aliases: asset class | asset classes | types of assets | financial assets | what is an asset

32.title: Bonds
32.summary: A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays interest and returns the amount borrowed on a set date. Its market price moves in the opposite direction to interest rates.
32.aliases: bond | fixed income | government bonds | corporate bonds | bond yield | coupon

33.title: Buyers, Sellers & Price
33.summary: A price is the level of the most recent trade between a buyer and a seller. It moves when one side becomes more willing to accept the other side's terms.
33.aliases: how price is set | why prices move | bid and ask basics | more buyers than sellers

34.title: Commodities
34.summary: Commodities are standardised raw materials such as oil, gold, copper and wheat. They trade in physical markets and, more visibly, through futures contracts.
34.aliases: commodity | raw materials | commodity markets | gold and oil | hard and soft commodities

35.title: ETFs & Indexes
35.summary: An index is a calculated number that tracks a defined group of assets. An ETF is a fund whose shares trade on an exchange, and most ETFs are built to follow an index.
35.aliases: ETF | exchange-traded fund | index | stock index | index fund | indices

36.title: Exchanges & Brokers
36.summary: An exchange is a venue where buy and sell orders are matched under published rules. A broker is an intermediary that gives customers access to that venue and handles their orders.
36.aliases: exchange | stock exchange | broker | brokerage | clearing house | settlement

37.title: Forex & Currency Pairs
37.summary: Forex is the market where currencies are exchanged for one another. A quote such as EUR/USD gives the price of one unit of the first currency in terms of the second.
37.aliases: forex | FX | foreign exchange | currency pairs | EUR/USD | base and quote currency | pip

38.title: Stocks & Shares
38.summary: A share is one unit of ownership in a company. Stocks trade on exchanges, and their prices reflect what buyers and sellers currently agree the company's shares are worth.
38.aliases: stocks | shares | equities | equity | what is a stock | common stock

39.title: Supply & Demand
39.summary: Supply is how much of something sellers offer at each price, demand is how much buyers want at each price, and the market price settles where the two balance.
39.aliases: supply and demand | law of supply and demand | equilibrium price | market equilibrium

40.title: Volatility
40.summary: Volatility is a measure of how large an asset's price moves are over a period. It describes the size of the swings, not their direction.
40.aliases: volatile | price volatility | historical volatility | implied volatility | realized volatility

41.title: Trading Volume Explained
41.summary: Trading volume is the number of units of an asset that changed hands in a period. Every unit counted was bought by one party and sold by another.
41.aliases: trading volume | volume | 24h volume | what is volume | buy volume and sell volume

42.title: What Is a Market?
42.summary: A market is any place or system where buyers and sellers meet to exchange something at a price they both accept.
42.aliases: market | financial market | markets explained | what is a financial market

43.title: What Is a Crypto Wallet?
43.summary: A crypto wallet is software or a device that stores and uses the private keys controlling funds on a blockchain. The coins themselves are records on the blockchain, not files in the wallet.
43.aliases: crypto wallet | wallet | blockchain wallet | digital wallet | bitcoin wallet

44.title: Bull, Bear, Long & Short Explained
44.summary: Bull and bear describe a market or an opinion about it, while long and short describe a position someone holds. Keeping the two pairs apart removes a very common beginner confusion.
44.aliases: bull bear long short | bullish vs long | bearish vs short | four market words | market direction words

45.title: How to Read Chart Patterns
45.summary: A chart pattern is a named summary of how price behaved across several swing points. Patterns describe structure; they are subjective, probabilistic and much clearer in hindsight.
45.aliases: chart patterns | price patterns | chart formations | classical chart patterns

46.title: Candle Anatomy
46.summary: A candle packs four prices from one period, the open, high, low and close, into a single shape made of a body and two wicks.
46.aliases: candlestick anatomy | parts of a candle | OHLC | real body and shadows

47.title: How Indicators Work
47.summary: A technical indicator is a calculation applied to past price and volume data, drawn on the chart to make one aspect of market behaviour easier to see.
47.aliases: technical indicators | chart indicators | indicator basics | overlays | oscillators

48.title: What Is Risk Management?
48.summary: Risk management is the set of decisions, made before the outcome is known, that limit how much a single trade or a whole account can lose.
48.aliases: risk management | money management | risk control | capital preservation

49.title: How a Trade Works
49.summary: A trade starts as an order, becomes a fill when it is matched with another trader's order, lives as an open position, and ends when that position is closed.
49.aliases: life of a trade | trade lifecycle | how trading works | order to fill

50.title: Spot Trading
50.summary: Spot trading is buying or selling the asset itself, paid for in full and delivered straight away, with no borrowing, no leverage and no liquidation.
50.aliases: spot market | spot | spot price | cash market | trading pair | base and quote

51.title: Chart Interface Basics
51.summary: A charting screen is built from a few standard parts: a price pane, a time axis, a price axis, symbol and timeframe selectors, drawing tools, indicator panes and a watchlist.
51.aliases: chart layout | parts of a chart | tradingview interface | chart screen | how to read a chart screen

52.title: Gas & Network Fees
52.summary: A network fee is what a blockchain charges to process a transaction. On Ethereum-style chains it is measured in gas: the fee is the gas used multiplied by the price per unit of gas.
52.aliases: gas | gas fee | gas fees | network fee | transaction fee | gwei | base fee | priority fee | gas limit | EIP-1559

53.title: Liquidity Providers
53.summary: Liquidity providers deposit both tokens of a pair into a liquidity pool so that others can trade against it, and receive a share of the swap fees while carrying the pool's risks.
53.aliases: LP | LPs | liquidity provider | liquidity provision | providing liquidity | LP token | LP tokens | liquidity mining | yield farming

54.title: Overtrading
54.summary: Overtrading is trading more often, in larger size or in more markets than a person's own plan and capital support, usually driven by emotion and not opportunity.
54.aliases: overtrading | over-trading | trading too much | churning | excessive trading | boredom trading

55.title: Trading Fees: Maker & Taker
55.summary: Exchanges charge a fee on each fill: the maker rate applies to orders that add resting liquidity to the book and the taker rate to orders that remove it.
55.aliases: maker fee | taker fee | maker and taker | trading fee | exchange fees | commission | fee tier

56.title: Custodial & Non-Custodial Wallets
56.summary: In a custodial wallet a company holds the private keys for its customers. In a non-custodial wallet the user holds them. The difference decides who can move, freeze or lose the funds.
56.aliases: custodial wallet | non-custodial wallet | self-custody | self custody | not your keys not your coins | exchange wallet

57.title: Hot & Cold Wallets
57.summary: A hot wallet keeps private keys on an internet-connected device, and a cold wallet keeps them offline. The trade-off is convenience against exposure to remote attacks.
57.aliases: hot wallet | cold wallet | cold storage | offline wallet | air-gapped wallet | paper wallet

58.title: Private Keys
58.summary: A private key is a secret number that authorises spending from a blockchain address. Whoever has the key controls the funds, and nobody can reset or reissue it.
58.aliases: private key | secret key | public key | key pair | public and private keys

59.title: Seed Phrases
59.summary: A seed phrase is a list of words, commonly 12 or 24, from which a wallet can regenerate all of its private keys. It is the master secret and the only backup of the wallet.
59.aliases: seed phrase | recovery phrase | mnemonic phrase | secret recovery phrase | backup phrase | 12 words | 24 words | BIP-39

60.title: Hot Wallet vs Cold Wallet
60.summary: A hot wallet keeps its keys on a device connected to the internet. A cold wallet keeps them offline. The trade-off is between convenience and exposure to remote attack.
60.aliases: hot vs cold wallet | hot storage vs cold storage | cold wallet vs hot wallet | online vs offline wallet

61.title: Addresses & Sending Safely
61.summary: An address is a public identifier, derived from a public key, that funds are sent to. Blockchain transfers cannot be recalled, so the address and the network both have to be right before sending.
61.aliases: wallet address | public address | address poisoning | wrong network | memo | destination tag | test transaction

62.title: Smart Contract Risk
62.summary: Smart contract risk is the chance that the code holding funds in a blockchain application fails, is exploited or is changed, causing a loss that usually cannot be reversed.
62.aliases: contract risk | protocol risk | DeFi exploit | smart contract exploit | smart contract audit | admin key | upgrade key | oracle manipulation | reentrancy

63.title: Exchange Account Security
63.summary: Exchange account security is the set of protections around a custodial account: a unique password, a strong second factor, a secured email address and, where offered, withdrawal allow-lists and anti-phishing codes.
63.aliases: exchange security | account security | withdrawal whitelist | withdrawal allow-list | address whitelisting | anti-phishing code | account takeover | API key security

64.title: Fake Airdrops & Wallet Drainers
64.summary: A fake airdrop lures people to a website with the promise of tokens to claim. There a wallet drainer presents signature requests that hand the attacker control of the assets in the wallet.
64.aliases: fake airdrop | wallet drainer | drainer | airdrop scam | claim scam | dust attack | scam token | fake mint

65.title: Fake Support & Impersonation
65.summary: Fake support is a scam in which someone poses as a help desk, company employee, official or public figure to obtain a seed phrase, a login code, remote access to a device or a payment.
65.aliases: fake support | support scam | impersonation scam | fake admin | giveaway scam | safe wallet scam | recovery scam

66.title: Hardware Wallets
66.summary: A hardware wallet is a small dedicated device that stores private keys offline and signs transactions on the device itself, so the keys never reach the computer or phone it is used with.
66.aliases: hardware wallet | signing device | cold wallet device | blind signing | secure element

67.title: Phishing
67.summary: Phishing is an attack that imitates a trusted service to trick a person into giving up a secret or signing a harmful request. In crypto the target is usually a seed phrase, a login or a signature.
67.aliases: phishing attack | phishing site | fake website | spoofed site | scam link | smishing

68.title: Pump and Dump
68.summary: A pump and dump is a scheme in which insiders buy an asset cheaply, promote it to drive the price up, and sell to the latecomers the promotion attracted, after which the price collapses.
68.aliases: pump and dump | pump-and-dump | P&D | pump group | pump scheme | exit liquidity | shilling

69.title: Rug Pulls & Honeypots
69.summary: A rug pull is when a project's developers abandon it and remove the liquidity or funds, leaving holders with a token they cannot sell for value. A honeypot is a token that can be bought but not sold.
69.aliases: rug pull | rugpull | rug | honeypot | honeypot token | exit scam | liquidity pull | soft rug

70.title: Security Checklist
70.summary: A practical checklist of security habits for wallets and exchange accounts: protecting the seed phrase, checking addresses, reading what is signed and recognising the common scams.
70.aliases: crypto security checklist | wallet security checklist | security habits | crypto safety | security best practices

71.title: Signing Transactions
71.summary: Signing uses a private key to authorise a transaction or message. The signature is the consent, so a malicious request that gets signed can hand over assets without the seed phrase ever being revealed.
71.aliases: signing | digital signature | sign a transaction | message signing | signature request | blind signing | permit signature

72.title: Token Approvals
72.summary: A token approval gives a smart contract standing permission to spend a specific token from a wallet, often an unlimited amount, and it stays in force until it is revoked.
72.aliases: token approval | allowance | token allowance | unlimited approval | infinite approval | revoke approval | set approval for all | ERC-20 approve

73.title: Two-Factor Authentication
73.summary: Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second proof of identity to a password when signing in. Authenticator apps and hardware security keys are generally stronger second factors than SMS codes.
73.aliases: 2FA | two-factor authentication | two-step verification | MFA | multi-factor authentication | authenticator app | security key | SIM swap | TOTP | passkey

74.title: Market Cap & Fully Diluted Valuation
74.summary: Market cap is price multiplied by circulating supply. Fully diluted valuation (FDV) is price multiplied by max or total supply, showing the size implied if every unit existed today.
74.aliases: market cap | market capitalization | market capitalisation | FDV | fully diluted valuation | fully diluted market cap | mcap

75.title: Token Supply: Circulating, Total & Max
75.summary: Circulating supply is the number of units in public circulation, total supply is the number that exist now, and max supply is the hard cap, if the asset has one.
75.aliases: circulating supply | total supply | max supply | maximum supply | supply cap | token burn | float

76.title: Token Unlocks & Emissions
76.summary: A token unlock releases existing locked tokens to their owners on a schedule, while emissions create new tokens over time as rewards. Both increase the supply that can be traded.
76.aliases: token unlock | unlock schedule | vesting | vesting schedule | cliff | emissions | token emissions | inflation schedule

77.title: Tokenomics
77.summary: Tokenomics is the economic design of a token: how many units exist, who receives them and when, what the token is used for, and what adds to or removes from its supply.
77.aliases: token economics | token design | token distribution | token allocation | token model

78.title: Market Capitalization
78.summary: Market capitalization is the current price of one unit multiplied by the number of units outstanding. It measures size at the latest price, not the amount of money invested.
78.aliases: market cap | mcap | market capitalisation | large cap | small cap | market value

79.title: Resistance
79.summary: Resistance is a price area above the market where selling interest has repeatedly been strong enough to pause or reverse an advance. It may hold again, and it may not.
79.aliases: resistance level | resistance zone | resistance area | price ceiling | supply zone | overhead supply

80.title: Market Cap vs Fully Diluted Valuation
80.summary: Market cap is price times the supply circulating today. Fully diluted valuation (FDV) is price times the maximum supply, which assumes today's price would hold for every future unit.
80.aliases: market cap vs fdv | fdv vs market cap | fully diluted valuation | fdv | mcap vs fdv | fully diluted market cap

81.title: Staking
81.summary: Staking means locking tokens to help secure a proof-of-stake blockchain in exchange for rewards, while accepting lock-up periods, slashing risk and changes in the token's price.
81.aliases: stake | staked | staking rewards | validator staking | delegation | delegated staking | liquid staking | liquid staking token | LST | unbonding | slashing

82.title: Ethereum: An Overview
82.summary: Ethereum is a public blockchain, launched in 2015, that runs programs called smart contracts. Its native asset is ether (ETH), which normally pays for each transaction on the network.
82.aliases: Ethereum | ETH | ether | EVM | Ethereum Virtual Machine | the Merge

83.title: Coins & Tokens
83.summary: A coin is the native asset of its own blockchain, while a token is issued by a smart contract that runs on an existing blockchain and relies on that chain's coin for fees.
83.aliases: coin vs token | native coin | native asset | crypto token | ERC-20 | token contract

84.title: What Is DeFi?
84.summary: DeFi, short for decentralized finance, is the collective name for financial services such as trading, lending and borrowing that run as smart contracts on public blockchains.
84.aliases: DeFi | decentralized finance | decentralised finance | open finance | DeFi protocol | composability

85.title: What Is Market Structure?
85.summary: Market structure is the pattern of swing highs and swing lows that price leaves behind. It describes whether a market is trending up, trending down or moving sideways.
85.aliases: market structure | price structure | trend structure

86.title: Support & Resistance Basics
86.summary: Support and resistance are price areas where buying or selling interest has repeatedly appeared. Support sits below price, resistance sits above, and neither is an exact line or a guarantee.
86.aliases: support and resistance | S/R | S&R | key levels | price levels

87.title: Airdrops
87.summary: An airdrop is a distribution of tokens to many wallet addresses, usually without payment, often to reward early users or spread ownership. The format is widely imitated by scams.
87.aliases: airdrop | token airdrop | retroactive airdrop | airdrop claim | snapshot | airdrop farming

88.title: Altcoins
88.summary: Altcoin is a loose label for any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin, covering thousands of assets with very different purposes, designs, liquidity and risks.
88.aliases: altcoin | alts | alternative coins | bitcoin dominance | altcoin season

89.title: A Market That Never Closes
89.summary: Crypto markets trade 24 hours a day, every day of the year, with no opening bell, closing price or weekend break. That changes how candles, liquidity and risk behave.
89.aliases: crypto market hours | 24/7 market | 24/7 trading | crypto trading hours | daily close | weekend trading

90.title: Governance & Utility Tokens
90.summary: A governance token carries votes over a protocol's rules or treasury, and a utility token is needed to use a service. Many tokens combine both roles, and neither role is a claim on profits.
90.aliases: governance token | utility token | DAO | DAO token | voting token | on-chain governance | token voting

91.title: Meme Coins
91.summary: A meme coin is a crypto asset built around a joke, image or online community instead of a stated function. Its price depends almost entirely on attention and can change violently.
91.aliases: meme coin | memecoin | memecoins | meme token | joke coin

92.title: Stablecoins
92.summary: A stablecoin is a token designed to track a reference value, usually one U.S. dollar, using reserves, crypto collateral or an algorithm, each with its own way of failing.
92.aliases: stablecoin | stable coin | pegged token | USDT | USDC | DAI | peg | depeg

93.title: Market Cycles
93.summary: A market cycle is a descriptive model with four phases: accumulation, advance, distribution and decline. The phases are clear in hindsight and cannot be timed reliably.
93.aliases: market cycle | four phases of a market | accumulation and distribution | markup and markdown | boom and bust

94.title: Liquidity
94.summary: Liquidity is how easily an asset can be bought or sold, in the size you want, without the trade itself moving the price.
94.aliases: liquid market | illiquid | market depth | thin market | deep market

95.title: Market Makers & Liquidity Providers
95.summary: A market maker continuously quotes a price to buy and a price to sell an asset, earning the spread between them in exchange for carrying the risk of holding inventory.
95.aliases: market maker | MM | liquidity provider | LP | dealer | designated market maker

96.title: Order Book
96.summary: An order book is the live list of all waiting buy and sell orders for one market, sorted by price, from which the exchange matches trades.
96.aliases: orderbook | limit order book | market depth | depth of market | DOM | level 2

97.title: Slippage
97.summary: Slippage is the difference between the price a trader expected when sending an order and the price at which the order was actually filled.
97.aliases: price slippage | execution slippage | slippage tolerance | price impact | negative slippage | positive slippage

98.title: Technical & Fundamental Analysis
98.summary: Technical analysis studies price and volume history. Fundamental analysis studies the underlying business or asset. They ask different questions, and neither produces certainty.
98.aliases: technical analysis | fundamental analysis | TA | FA | TA vs FA | chart analysis

99.title: Anchoring
99.summary: Anchoring is the tendency to rely too heavily on one reference number, such as a purchase price or a past high, when judging what a price is worth now.
99.aliases: anchoring | anchoring bias | anchor price | price anchoring | unit bias | anchoring and adjustment

100.title: Liquidation Cascades
100.summary: A liquidation cascade is a chain reaction in which forced closures of leveraged positions push the price further, which triggers more forced closures.
100.aliases: liquidation cascade | cascading liquidations | long squeeze | liquidation spiral | forced selling | liquidation heatmap

101.title: Broadening Formation
101.summary: A broadening formation is a series of higher highs and lower lows, so the swings grow and the boundary lines spread apart. It describes expanding volatility with neither side in control.
101.aliases: megaphone pattern | broadening top | broadening pattern | expanding triangle | megaphone

102.title: Gaps
102.summary: A gap is an empty space on a chart where no trades took place, because price jumped from one level to another between two candles. Gaps are common in stocks and rare in 24-hour crypto markets.
102.aliases: price gap | gap up | gap down | window | gap fill | breakaway gap | exhaustion gap

103.title: Inside Bar & Outside Bar
103.summary: An inside bar is a candle whose whole range sits within the previous candle's range. An outside bar exceeds the previous range on both sides. One shows contraction, the other expansion.
103.aliases: inside bar | outside bar | inside day | outside day | mother bar

104.title: Long-Legged Doji
104.summary: A Long-Legged Doji has long wicks on both sides and an open and close that are almost equal. Price swung widely and ended where it began.

105.title: ATR (Average True Range)
105.summary: ATR is a volatility indicator that shows the average size of recent candles, including gaps, in price units. It measures how much price moves, not which way.
105.aliases: ATR | Average True Range | true range | ATR 14 | ATR percent

106.title: Bollinger Bands
106.summary: Bollinger Bands are a 20-period moving average with an upper and a lower band set two standard deviations away, so the bands widen and narrow as volatility changes.
106.aliases: BB | Bollinger | Bollinger squeeze | BBands | %B | BandWidth | volatility bands

107.title: Donchian Channels
107.summary: Donchian Channels plot the highest high and the lowest low of the last N periods, so the band shows the full price range the market has covered recently.
107.aliases: Donchian Channel | price channel | Donchian bands | 20-period high and low

108.title: Keltner Channels
108.summary: Keltner Channels are a volatility envelope: an exponential moving average with an upper and a lower line placed a multiple of the Average True Range away from it.
108.aliases: Keltner Channel | Keltner bands | KC | ATR channel

109.title: Supertrend
109.summary: Supertrend is a trend-following line built from the Average True Range that trails below price in rising phases and flips above price when a candle closes through it.
109.aliases: SuperTrend | Super Trend | ATR trailing line | Supertrend 10 3

110.title: Stop Placement
110.summary: Stop placement is the choice of the price at which a trade idea is treated as wrong, and it sets the stop distance that position sizing depends on.
110.aliases: where to put a stop | stop distance | stop level | ATR stop | structure stop | invalidation level

111.title: Stablecoin Risks
111.summary: Stablecoins aim to hold a fixed value and can fail to: reserves can be weaker than claimed, redemption can be limited, market prices can de-peg and algorithmic designs can collapse.
111.aliases: de-peg | depeg | depegging | stablecoin de-peg | peg | stablecoin reserves | algorithmic stablecoin | stablecoin collapse | redemption risk

112.title: DeFi Lending & Borrowing
112.summary: DeFi lending protocols pool tokens from suppliers and lend them to borrowers who post more collateral than they borrow. If the collateral's value falls too far, the loan is liquidated.
112.aliases: DeFi lending | lending protocol | money market | over-collateralized loan | overcollateralized | health factor | loan-to-value | LTV | liquidation threshold | utilization rate

113.title: Margin on Derivatives
113.summary: Margin on derivatives is the collateral posted to open and keep a position: initial margin opens it, and maintenance margin is the minimum needed to keep it open.
113.aliases: initial margin | maintenance margin | margin balance | margin ratio | maintenance margin rate | futures margin

114.title: Margin & Collateral
114.summary: Margin is the collateral posted to open and keep a leveraged position; it absorbs the position's losses, and if it falls below the maintenance requirement the position is liquidated.
114.aliases: margin | collateral | initial margin | maintenance margin | margin ratio | margin balance | equity | free margin

115.title: AMMs & Liquidity Pools
115.summary: An automated market maker (AMM) prices trades with a formula applied to a pool of two tokens, instead of matching buyers and sellers in an order book.
115.aliases: AMM | AMMs | automated market maker | liquidity pool | liquidity pools | constant product | constant product formula | price impact

116.title: APR & APY
116.summary: APR is a yearly rate that leaves compounding out, and APY is a yearly rate that includes it, so the same underlying rate gives a higher APY than APR.
116.aliases: APR | APY | annual percentage rate | annual percentage yield | compounding | compound interest | yield

117.title: Decentralized Exchanges (DEX)
117.summary: A decentralized exchange is a set of smart contracts on a blockchain that lets people trade tokens directly from their own wallets, with no company holding their funds.
117.aliases: DEX | DEXs | decentralised exchange | on-chain exchange | non-custodial exchange

118.title: Impermanent Loss
118.summary: Impermanent loss is the gap between the value of tokens held in a liquidity pool and the value of simply holding them, which opens whenever their relative price changes.
118.aliases: IL | divergence loss | impermanent loss formula | LP loss

119.title: Swaps & Routing
119.summary: A swap exchanges one token for another through liquidity pools. Routing chooses which pools to use, and slippage tolerance sets the worst result the trader accepts before the swap reverts.
119.aliases: swap | token swap | routing | DEX aggregator | slippage tolerance | minimum received | multi-hop swap | sandwich attack

120.title: TVL (Total Value Locked)
120.summary: Total value locked (TVL) is the current market value of the assets deposited in a DeFi protocol's smart contracts. It moves with token prices as well as with deposits.
120.aliases: TVL | total value locked | value locked | DeFi TVL

121.title: CEX vs DEX
121.summary: A centralized exchange (CEX) is a company that holds customer assets and matches trades. A decentralized exchange (DEX) is a set of smart contracts that users trade against from their own wallets.
121.aliases: centralized vs decentralized exchange | cex or dex | dex vs cex | centralised exchange vs decentralised exchange

122.title: APR vs APY
122.summary: APR is a yearly rate without compounding. APY is the yearly rate with compounding included. For the same underlying rate, APY is the higher number.
122.aliases: apy vs apr | apr or apy | annual percentage rate vs annual percentage yield | apr and apy difference

123.title: Centralized Exchanges (CEX)
123.summary: A centralized exchange is a company that runs a crypto market: it holds customers' funds, records their balances in its own ledger and matches their buy and sell orders.
123.aliases: CEX | centralised exchange | crypto exchange | custodial exchange | exchange account

124.title: Counterparty Risk
124.summary: Counterparty risk is the risk that the other party to an arrangement, such as an exchange, a lender or a token issuer, cannot or will not do what it promised.
124.aliases: counterparty | default risk | credit risk | custodial risk | exchange risk | exchange insolvency | proof of reserves | rehypothecation

125.title: Arbitrage
125.summary: Arbitrage is buying an asset where it is cheaper and selling the same asset where it is dearer. The trading itself tends to remove the price difference.
125.aliases: arb | arbitrageur | price difference between exchanges | law of one price | triangular arbitrage

126.title: Custodial vs Non-Custodial
126.summary: With a custodial wallet, a third party holds the private keys on the user's behalf. With a non-custodial wallet, the user holds the keys and carries the full responsibility.
126.aliases: custodial vs self-custody | self-custody | non-custodial wallet | custodial wallet | not your keys not your coins

127.title: Liquidation on Perpetuals
127.summary: Liquidation on perpetuals is the forced closing of a leveraged position by the exchange when its margin balance, measured at the mark price, falls to the maintenance margin.
127.aliases: perp liquidation | liquidation price | bankruptcy price | insurance fund | auto-deleveraging | ADL | liquidation engine

128.title: Risk, Psychology & Trading Styles
128.summary: How position sizing, risk/reward and drawdown work, why emotions such as FOMO and revenge trading distort decisions, and how the main trading styles differ.
128.aliases: chapter 9 | risk management basics | trading psychology basics | trading styles overview

129.title: Hedging Basics
129.summary: Hedging means reducing exposure to a price move by holding an offsetting position. It lowers both losses and gains, and it has costs and risks of its own, so it is not free protection.
129.aliases: hedge | hedging | hedged position | delta neutral | hedge ratio | offsetting position

130.title: Short Position
130.summary: A short position is one that gains value if the price falls and loses value if it rises. It relies on borrowing or on a derivative contract, and its possible loss is not capped.
130.aliases: short | going short | short selling | shorting | short trade | short sale

131.title: Pattern Failure & Invalidation
131.summary: Chart patterns fail often. Invalidation is the condition, stated in advance, under which a pattern reading no longer fits the chart, and a failed pattern is information about the market, not an error.
131.aliases: failed pattern | pattern failure | invalidation | bull trap | bear trap

132.title: Concentration Risk
132.summary: Concentration risk is the danger that comes from having a large share of capital depend on a single asset, theme, venue or outcome.
132.aliases: concentration risk | concentrated position | single asset risk | all eggs in one basket | portfolio weight

133.title: Diversification & Correlation
133.summary: Diversification spreads capital across holdings that do not all move together. Correlation, from -1 to +1, measures how closely two of them have moved together.
133.aliases: diversification | correlation | correlation coefficient | correlated positions | portfolio risk

134.title: Drawdown
134.summary: A drawdown is the decline of an account or an asset from a peak to a later low, measured as a percentage of the peak.
134.aliases: drawdown | max drawdown | maximum drawdown | MDD | peak to trough | underwater

135.title: Leverage Risk
135.summary: Leverage risk is the way borrowed exposure multiplies losses on a trader's own capital and adds the possibility of forced closure, called liquidation.
135.aliases: leverage risk | risk of leverage | leveraged trading risk | effective leverage | over-leverage

136.title: Position Sizing
136.summary: Position sizing is the calculation of how large a trade can be so that the loss at the planned stop equals the amount chosen as risk per trade.
136.aliases: position size | trade size | lot size | position size calculation | percent risk model

137.title: Risk of Ruin
137.summary: Risk of ruin is the probability that an account falls to a level where trading cannot continue, given a win rate, a payoff ratio and a risk per trade.
137.aliases: risk of ruin | probability of ruin | gambler's ruin | ruin probability | blowing up an account

138.title: Risk Per Trade
138.summary: Risk per trade is the amount an account would lose if one trade is closed at its planned stop, usually expressed as a percentage of the account.
138.aliases: risk per trade | account risk | 1% rule | 2% rule | fixed fractional risk

139.title: Risk/Reward Ratio
139.summary: The risk/reward ratio compares the planned loss on a trade, from entry to stop, with the planned gain, from entry to target.
139.aliases: risk reward ratio | risk to reward | R:R | RR | reward to risk | R-multiple

140.title: Trading Journal
140.summary: A trading journal is a record of each trade's reasoning, risk, result and circumstances, kept so that decisions can be reviewed against evidence and not memory.
140.aliases: trading journal | trade journal | trade log | trading diary | trade record

141.title: Trading Plan
141.summary: A trading plan is a written set of rules, made in advance, that describes what a person trades, when, how much is at risk and how each trade ends.
141.aliases: trading plan | trade plan | trading rules | rule-based trading | trading checklist

142.title: Win Rate & Expectancy
142.summary: Win rate is the share of trades that end in a gain. Expectancy combines it with the average size of wins and losses to give the average result per trade.
142.aliases: win rate | hit rate | expectancy | expected value | edge | profit factor

143.title: Isolated & Cross Margin
143.summary: Isolated margin normally confines a position's loss to the margin assigned to it, while cross margin lets positions draw on the whole account balance as shared collateral.
143.aliases: isolated margin | cross margin | margin mode | cross-margin | shared margin | portfolio margin

144.title: Leverage
144.summary: Leverage is the ratio of a position's size to the margin backing it; it multiplies the effect of every price move on that margin, for losses exactly as much as for gains.
144.aliases: leveraged trading | 10x | leverage ratio | notional value | effective leverage | gearing

145.title: Liquidation
145.summary: Liquidation is the forced closing of a leveraged position by the exchange when the margin behind it falls below the maintenance requirement.
145.aliases: liquidated | liquidation price | forced liquidation | forced close | margin call | getting liquidated | bankruptcy price

146.title: Margin Trading
146.summary: Margin trading means trading with funds borrowed from an exchange or broker against collateral, which enlarges a position and multiplies both its gains and its losses.
146.aliases: trading on margin | margin account | spot margin | buying on margin | margin loan | margin call

147.title: Stop Loss
147.summary: A stop loss is a stop order placed in advance to close a position if price moves against it to a chosen level, limiting the loss approximately but not exactly.
147.aliases: stop-loss | stop loss order | SL | protective stop | stopped out | mental stop

148.title: Day Trading
148.summary: Day trading is a style in which positions are opened and closed within the same day, so nothing is held overnight. It demands hours of attention and many trades.
148.aliases: day trader | intraday trading | daytrading | intraday

149.title: Stop Loss vs Liquidation
149.summary: A stop loss is the trader's own planned exit order. Liquidation is a forced close by the exchange when margin no longer covers the loss. One is chosen, the other is imposed.
149.aliases: liquidation vs stop loss | stop loss or liquidation | stop vs liquidation price | stop-loss vs liquidation

150.title: Mark Price & Index Price
150.summary: The index price is an average of spot prices across several exchanges, and the mark price is the reference price built from it that is used for unrealized P&L and liquidation.
150.aliases: mark price | index price | last price | fair price | fair price marking | mark vs last price

151.title: Short Squeeze
151.summary: A short squeeze is a fast price rise in which short sellers are forced to buy back their positions, and their buying pushes the price higher still. This page explains the mechanism only.
151.aliases: short squeeze | squeeze | short covering rally | short covering | long squeeze

152.title: Isolated vs Cross Margin
152.summary: Isolated margin normally limits the loss on a position to the margin assigned to it. Cross margin backs every position with the shared account balance, so one position can draw on all of it.
152.aliases: cross vs isolated margin | isolated margin | cross margin | isolated or cross | margin mode

153.title: Spot vs Perpetuals
153.summary: Spot trading means buying and owning the asset itself. A perpetual is a leveraged contract that tracks the asset's price, with funding payments and the risk of liquidation.
153.aliases: spot vs futures | spot vs perps | spot or perpetual | spot trading vs perpetual futures | perps vs spot

154.title: Market Order vs Limit Order
154.summary: A market order trades immediately at the best prices available. A limit order trades only at a chosen price or better, and may not trade at all.
154.aliases: market vs limit | limit order vs market order | limit or market order | market order or limit order

155.title: Funding Rate
155.summary: The funding rate is a periodic payment exchanged between long and short holders of a perpetual future that pulls the contract price toward the spot index.
155.aliases: funding | funding rates | funding payment | funding fee | perp funding | positive funding | negative funding

156.title: Long/Short Ratio
156.summary: The long/short ratio compares long and short positioning in a derivatives market, usually by counting accounts, which is not the same as measuring position size.
156.aliases: long short ratio | L/S ratio | long/short accounts ratio | top trader long/short ratio | taker buy/sell ratio

157.title: Open Interest
157.summary: Open interest is the total number, or value, of derivative contracts that are currently open and have not yet been closed or settled.
157.aliases: OI | open contracts | outstanding contracts | futures open interest | notional open interest

158.title: Crypto Markets and Stock Markets
158.summary: Stock markets have set trading hours, closing auctions and separate brokers, exchanges and clearing houses. Crypto spot markets trade around the clock on platforms that often combine those roles.
158.aliases: crypto vs stocks | crypto market vs stock market | stocks vs crypto | 24/7 trading | differences between crypto and stocks

159.title: Interest Rates & Inflation
159.summary: Inflation is a general rise in prices that reduces what money can buy. Interest rates are the price of borrowing money, and central banks adjust their policy rates largely in response to inflation.
159.aliases: interest rates | inflation | central bank | policy rate | purchasing power | real interest rate | CPI

160.title: Basis, Contango & Backwardation
160.summary: Basis is the futures price minus the spot price: contango means futures trade above spot, and backwardation means futures trade below spot.
160.aliases: basis | contango | backwardation | futures premium | futures curve | cost of carry | cash and carry

161.title: Futures Contracts
161.summary: A futures contract is a standardised agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a set future date, traded on an exchange and backed by margin.
161.aliases: futures | future | dated futures | futures contract | expiry | cash settlement | physical delivery

162.title: Perpetual Futures
162.summary: A perpetual future is a futures contract with no expiry date that uses funding payments between longs and shorts to keep its price close to the spot index.
162.aliases: perpetuals | perps | perp | perpetual swap | perpetual contract | perpetual futures contract

163.title: Market Structure
163.summary: How swing highs and swing lows reveal whether a market is in an uptrend, a downtrend or a range, and what a change between those states looks like.
163.aliases: chapter 4 | market structure basics | higher highs and higher lows | trend structure

164.title: Break of Structure
164.summary: A break of structure is the moment price moves beyond a swing point that defined the trend. In an uptrend it is commonly defined as a close below the most recent higher low.
164.aliases: BOS | structure break | market structure break | change of character | market structure shift

165.title: Downtrend
165.summary: A downtrend is a sequence of lower swing highs and lower swing lows. Price falls in steps, and each bounce ends below the high of the one before it.
165.aliases: down trend | bearish trend | lower highs and lower lows | falling trend

166.title: Multi-Timeframe Structure
166.summary: Multi-timeframe structure is the practice of reading the same market on several chart timeframes, because one market can be in an uptrend on one timeframe and a downtrend on another.
166.aliases: multiple timeframe analysis | MTF analysis | top-down analysis | higher timeframe | lower timeframe

167.title: Pullbacks & Corrections
167.summary: A pullback is a temporary move against the prevailing trend, and a correction is a larger or longer one. Both are a normal part of trends and are only confirmed as temporary in hindsight.
167.aliases: pullback | correction | retracement | dip | relief rally | reaction

168.title: Range
168.summary: A range is a period in which price moves sideways between an upper area and a lower area, making neither a series of higher highs and lows nor a series of lower ones.
168.aliases: trading range | sideways market | consolidation | ranging market

169.title: Swing Highs & Swing Lows
169.summary: A swing high is a peak with lower highs on both sides, and a swing low is a trough with higher lows on both sides. They are the turning points used to read market structure.
169.aliases: swing points | pivot highs and lows | peaks and troughs | fractals

170.title: Trend Transitions
170.summary: A trend transition is the process by which an uptrend or downtrend ends and turns into a range or the opposite trend. It usually unfolds over several swings, not in one candle.
170.aliases: trend change | trend reversal | change of trend | market turn

171.title: Trend Lines
171.summary: A trend line is a straight line drawn through successive swing lows in an uptrend or swing highs in a downtrend. It summarises the slope of a trend and marks a moving area that traders watch.
171.aliases: trendline | trendlines | trend line | diagonal support | diagonal resistance

172.title: Uptrend
172.summary: An uptrend is a sequence of higher swing highs and higher swing lows. Price climbs in steps, and each pullback ends above the low of the one before it.
172.aliases: up trend | bullish trend | higher highs and higher lows | rising trend

173.title: Bid, Ask & Spread
173.summary: The bid is the highest price a buyer is offering, the ask is the lowest price a seller will accept, and the spread is the gap between the two.
173.aliases: bid-ask spread | bid and ask | bid price | ask price | offer price | spread

174.title: Market Participants
174.summary: Market participants are the people and organisations that trade: investors, hedgers, speculators, arbitrageurs and market makers, each with different goals and time horizons.
174.aliases: who trades | retail traders | institutional investors | retail vs institutional | whales | smart money

175.title: Support
175.summary: Support is a price area below the market where buying interest has repeatedly been strong enough to pause or reverse a decline. It may hold again, and it may not.
175.aliases: support level | support zone | support area | price floor | demand zone

176.title: Charts & Timeframes
176.summary: How a chart compresses trading into open, high, low and close, how the main chart types differ, and why the chosen timeframe changes what you see.
176.aliases: chapter 2 | how to read a chart | chart basics | timeframes explained

177.title: Money Flow Index (MFI)
177.summary: The Money Flow Index is a 0-100 oscillator that applies the RSI idea to price multiplied by volume, so periods with heavy volume count for more than quiet ones.
177.aliases: MFI | Money Flow Index | volume-weighted RSI | money flow

178.title: OBV (On-Balance Volume)
178.summary: On-Balance Volume is a running total that adds a period's volume when price closes higher and subtracts it when price closes lower.
178.aliases: OBV | On-Balance Volume | on balance volume | Granville OBV

179.title: Volume Profile
179.summary: Volume profile is a sideways histogram that shows how much volume traded at each price level over a chosen period, instead of how much traded in each time period.
179.aliases: volume profile | volume by price | point of control | POC | value area | VPVR

180.title: Volume
180.summary: Volume is the amount of an asset traded during each candle, shown as bars beneath the price chart. It measures how much activity stood behind a price move.
180.aliases: trading volume | volume bars | volume indicator | relative volume | RVOL | volume moving average

181.title: VWAP
181.summary: VWAP (Volume-Weighted Average Price) is the average price traded during a session, with each price weighted by the volume traded at it.
181.aliases: Volume-Weighted Average Price | volume weighted average price | session VWAP | anchored VWAP | AVWAP

182.title: Breakouts
182.summary: A breakout is a move by price beyond a watched area, most often a close above a resistance zone or the edge of a range. It shows that the area gave way, not that the move continues.
182.aliases: breakout | price breakout | resistance break | range breakout | upside breakout

183.title: Markets & Crypto Basics
183.summary: What a market is, how buyers and sellers create a price, and the core vocabulary of volume, volatility, assets, exchanges, spot and derivatives.
183.aliases: chapter 1 | market basics | trading basics | how markets work

184.title: Support, Resistance & Breakouts
184.summary: How support and resistance zones form, what tests, breakouts, breakdowns, fakeouts and retests are, and why a level is an area and never a guarantee.
184.aliases: chapter 5 | support and resistance basics | breakouts and fakeouts | key levels

185.title: Descending Triangle
185.summary: A descending triangle is a flat line of lows beneath a falling line of highs. It shows sellers accepting less on each rally while buyers hold one level, and is conventionally read as bearish.
185.aliases: descending triangle pattern | falling triangle | flat-bottom triangle

186.title: Double Bottom
186.summary: A double bottom is two lows at a similar depth, separated by a bounce, that form after a decline. It is conventionally read as a possible reversal if the high between the lows breaks.
186.aliases: double bottom pattern | W pattern | W bottom

187.title: Breakdowns
187.summary: A breakdown is a move by price below a watched support area, most often judged by a close beneath it. It shows that buyers did not hold the area this time, not that the decline continues.
187.aliases: breakdown | support break | downside breakout | break of support | range breakdown

188.title: Confluence
188.summary: Confluence means several independent observations pointing to the same price area, such as a horizontal level, a trend line and a moving average meeting. It adds context, not certainty.
188.aliases: confluence zone | confluence of factors | confluent levels | stacked levels | cluster

189.title: Dynamic Support & Resistance
189.summary: Dynamic support and resistance are levels that move with time, such as moving averages and trend lines, in contrast to horizontal levels that stay at a fixed price.
189.aliases: dynamic support | dynamic resistance | moving support and resistance | moving average support | diagonal support and resistance

190.title: Role Reversal
190.summary: Role reversal is the tendency for a broken resistance area to act later as support, and for a broken support area to act later as resistance. It is a common observation, not a rule.
190.aliases: polarity principle | change of polarity | S/R flip | support turned resistance | resistance turned support

191.title: Round Numbers & Psychological Levels
191.summary: Round numbers such as 100 or 50,000 are prices that attract attention and orders simply because they are easy to think in. Traders often watch them as possible support or resistance.
191.aliases: round numbers | psychological levels | big figures | whole numbers | psychological support and resistance

192.title: Zones, Not Lines
192.summary: Support and resistance are better drawn as zones, bands of price, than as single lines, because markets rarely turn at exactly the same price twice.
192.aliases: support zone | resistance zone | price zones | areas of interest | levels as zones

193.title: Range Trading
193.summary: Range trading is an approach built on price moving back and forth between a support area and a resistance area. It relies on the boundaries holding, and every range eventually ends.
193.aliases: range trader | range-bound trading | trading ranges | sideways trading | range strategy

194.title: Support vs Resistance
194.summary: Support is a price area below the market where declines have tended to stop. Resistance is a price area above the market where advances have tended to stop.
194.aliases: support and resistance | resistance vs support | support or resistance | floor and ceiling

195.title: Confirmation Bias
195.summary: Confirmation bias is the tendency to look for, notice and remember information that supports what one already believes, and to discount what contradicts it.
195.aliases: confirmation bias | myside bias | cherry picking | echo chamber | selective evidence

196.title: Fear & Greed
196.summary: Fear and greed are the two emotions most often used to describe market behaviour: greed pushes people toward risk as prices rise, fear pushes them away as prices fall.
196.aliases: fear and greed | market sentiment | fear and greed index | euphoria | panic | capitulation

197.title: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out)
197.summary: FOMO is the anxious urge to join a price move because others appear to be profiting from it, usually after much of the move has already happened.
197.aliases: FOMO | fear of missing out | chasing price | chasing the market | FOMO buying

198.title: FUD (Fear, Uncertainty & Doubt)
198.summary: FUD is negative information, accurate or not, that spreads fear about an asset or market. The word is also used to wave away criticism that may be valid.
198.aliases: FUD | fear uncertainty and doubt | fear uncertainty doubt | spreading FUD | FUDster

199.title: Herd Behavior
199.summary: Herd behavior is the tendency of people to copy what a large group is doing, buying because others buy and selling because others sell, instead of judging independently.
199.aliases: herd behavior | herd behaviour | herding | herd mentality | crowd psychology | bandwagon effect | social proof

200.title: Loss Aversion
200.summary: Loss aversion is the tendency for a loss to hurt more than a gain of the same size pleases, which leads people to treat losing and winning positions differently.
200.aliases: loss aversion | prospect theory | disposition effect | holding losers | cutting winners | break-even effect

201.title: Overconfidence
201.summary: Overconfidence is the tendency to overrate one's own skill, knowledge or control over outcomes, which in trading leads to larger positions and thinner safety margins.
201.aliases: overconfidence | overconfidence bias | illusion of control | illusion of skill | self-attribution bias | hindsight bias

202.title: Patience & Discipline
202.summary: Patience is waiting until the conditions of a plan are met. Discipline is doing what the plan says once they are, including the parts that are uncomfortable.
202.aliases: patience | discipline | trading discipline | self-control | consistency | sitting on hands

203.title: Recency Bias
203.summary: Recency bias is the tendency to give the most recent events too much weight and to expect that what has just happened is what happens next.
203.aliases: recency bias | recency effect | availability bias | hot hand | gambler's fallacy | extrapolation

204.title: Revenge Trading
204.summary: Revenge trading is taking impulsive, often larger trades straight after a loss in an attempt to win the money back quickly.
204.aliases: revenge trading | revenge trade | tilt | trading on tilt | chasing losses

205.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
205.summary: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing with a decision because of the money, time or effort already spent on it, even though those costs cannot be recovered.
205.aliases: sunk cost fallacy | sunk cost | sunk cost effect | throwing good money after bad | averaging down | escalation of commitment

206.title: Why Psychology Matters
206.summary: Trading psychology is the study of how emotions and mental shortcuts shape decisions about money, and why knowing a rule is different from following it.
206.aliases: trading psychology | market psychology | emotional trading | mindset | behavioural finance

207.title: Options Basics
207.summary: An option is a contract that gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a set strike price by a set date.
207.aliases: options | option | call option | put option | calls and puts | strike price | option premium | option expiry

208.title: What Are Derivatives?
208.summary: A derivative is a contract whose value comes from the price of something else, called the underlying asset, rather than from owning that asset directly.
208.aliases: derivative | derivatives | derivative contract | underlying asset | financial derivatives

209.title: Long, Short & Position Mechanics
209.summary: How a position works from entry to exit: long and short, stop loss and take profit, realized and unrealized P&L, leverage, margin, liquidation and funding.
209.aliases: chapter 8 | position mechanics | how leverage works | long and short basics

210.title: Long Position
210.summary: A long position is one that gains value if the price rises and loses value if it falls. It can be as simple as owning an asset, or it can be a leveraged contract with very different risks.
210.aliases: long | going long | long trade | being long | long exposure

211.title: Bullish vs Bearish
211.summary: Bullish means expecting or describing rising prices, bearish means expecting or describing falling prices. Both are views or conditions, not positions.
211.aliases: bull vs bear | bullish or bearish | bull market vs bear market | bulls and bears
